meta.blurb: In the dead of night in the Chilean desert, a radio astronomer hears a pattern in the static, repeating again and again. Soon telescopes across the world hear it too. The first words they can read say: please answer.
meta.bible: Dr Ines Valdez: radio astronomer, patient and stubborn, listens to the sky at night. Kofi Adjei: young engineer and her night-shift partner, cheerful, good with cables. Anita Rao: director of the observatory, careful and fair. Dr Pavel Novak: mathematician in Prague who joins by video. Luz: Ines's nine-year-old niece, loves music. Dr Helen Ward: official of the national science agency, firm but kind. Atacama: the high, dry desert in Chile where the observatory stands. Chile. Tau Lyra: a faint star about 12 light years away, home of the Choir. The Choir: gentle beings who live as patterns of light and sound around Tau Lyra. The Song: everything the Choir knows, their history, stories and names. The relay: a small dark messenger object, the size of a bus, parked about a million kilometres from Earth, about three times as far as the Moon. Prague. Australia. Hawaii. Santiago. Moon. Earth. The pattern repeats every 73 seconds. The star Tau Lyra is old and growing cold; in about a hundred years the Choir will fade. A reply to Tau Lyra takes about 12 years each way. Voice and tone: calm, wondering and warm; science told simply; the aliens are kind, never a threat; no violence.

Kofi brought her tea, and she saw something strange on the screen.
The pattern came back again and again, like a heartbeat.
They checked every cable and machine, but nothing was wrong.
At sunrise, Ines told the director, but Anita Rao did not believe her.
Anita gave them three days to check, and to tell no one.
On the second day, a team in Australia heard it too.
Pavel, a number expert in Prague, found numbers hidden in the signal.
After the numbers came a picture of a star and planets.
Ines's niece Luz visited, and she listened to the sound.
Luz smiled and said that it was not noise, but a song.
Pavel agreed that the song repeated and taught with pictures.
Slowly they learned the first words: we, you, near, far, listen.
The news got out, and a woman from the government came.
Helen said no one could send an answer without permission.
At last they read a whole sentence: “Please answer us.”
Leaders argued about it, and Ines said, “Silence is also an answer.”
Helen agreed to send a small, kind reply to the stars.
At midnight, they sent their answer, and then they waited.
Four minutes later, an answer came, and it was far too fast.
Kofi did the sums and said the sender was very close.
A telescope in Hawaii found a small dark object nearby.
It was a black box, the size of a bus.
The world felt afraid, but Helen spoke in a calm voice.
The relay said its makers were called the Choir.
The Choir's star was old, and it was growing cold.
They did not ask for a home, only for someone to listen.
Their Song held all their stories, all their names and memories.
To copy the Song, they needed dishes from all over the world.
Anita called many people, and helpers began to come.
Helen's bosses were afraid, and they ordered the work to stop.
Ines flew to Santiago and played Helen a piece of the Song.
Helen heard a soft song like her mother's, and she changed her mind.
They agreed on three rules: be open, only listen, never touch.
For weeks, Kofi and the crews built the great new network.
The relay would be in view for only six hours.
On the last night, a storm broke a cable, so Kofi climbed up.
Luz pressed the big green button, and the dishes turned together.
The Song arrived like a river, and the copy began to fill.
The drives were filling up, so people shared their computers.
At seventy percent, the Choir sent a warning to them.
The last part was locked, and Luz's tune opened it.
The copy reached one hundred percent, and the room was silent.
The relay's small lights blinked, and the Choir said goodbye.
The last words said thank you, because they were heard.
People in many cities stopped in the street to listen.

Earth sent a song of its own to Tau Lyra.
Twenty-four years later, Luz stood by the same old dish.
Three soft notes came from the stars: “We hear you.”
B1B2: Dr Ines Valdez had worked the night shift in the Atacama desert for six years. Every night she listened to the hiss of the sky, and every night it said nothing.
Her young partner Kofi Adjei brought her a cup of tea at midnight. While she drank it, she noticed a tiny pattern hiding in the static from a faint star called Tau Lyra.
They watched the screen for an hour, and the pattern came back every 73 seconds. It was as steady as a heartbeat, and nothing in nature that they knew of was so regular.
Kofi changed the cables, restarted the computers and tested the dish. Nothing was broken, and the pattern was still there when he had finished.
At dawn Ines went to the director, Anita Rao, and told her everything. Anita listened carefully, but she had seen too many false alarms to be excited.
Anita agreed to give them three days of quiet checking. She asked other observatories to look at the same star without saying why.
On the second day a message arrived from Australia. Their dish had heard the same pattern, every 73 seconds, from exactly the same place in the sky.
Ines sent the data to Dr Pavel Novak, a mathematician in Prague. By evening he called her, almost shouting, because the pulses counted out the prime numbers: two, three, five, seven, eleven.
After the primes, the signal drew a simple picture made of dots. It showed a star with several planets, and one of them was marked as special.
That weekend Ines's nine-year-old niece Luz came to visit the observatory. Ines let her put on headphones and listen to the signal, sped up so that human ears could hear it.
Luz listened with her eyes closed and then looked up with a wide smile. She said that it was not a code at all, but a song, and a sad and hopeful one.
Pavel studied the notes and agreed that Luz was right. The tune repeated with small changes, and each phrase came with a picture, like a lesson for a child.
Over the next days the team learned the first words of the alien language. Soon they could read near, far, we, you and listen, and every new word felt like a door opening.
The secret did not stay secret for long, and within a week reporters crowded the gate. Dr Helen Ward arrived from the national science agency with a folder full of rules.
Helen Ward explained that nobody was allowed to reply to the signal without approval. Ines understood the need for care, but she worried that waiting might be dangerous.
One night, after weeks of hard work, Pavel finally decoded a whole sentence. It said that the senders had heard Earth's music for many years, and that they asked, kindly, for an answer.
In a long meeting, some leaders were afraid of what an answer might bring. Ines stood up and said that staying silent was also an answer, and perhaps a cold one.
In the end Helen Ward agreed to a short and gentle reply. Ines, Pavel and Luz wrote it together: the first prime numbers and a simple tune made by Luz.
At midnight the dish turned to the faint star and sent the reply. Then the team sat in the dark control room, wondering how many years it would take to hear anything back.
Less than four minutes later, the screen lit up with a brand new pattern. It was an answer, and it had come back impossibly fast.
Kofi wrote the numbers on the board and checked them twice. Light from Tau Lyra needs about twelve years to arrive, so whoever had answered must be very close to Earth.
Astronomers in Hawaii searched the sky where Kofi had pointed. They found a small, dark object about a million kilometres from Earth, which is about three times as far as the Moon.
The object was about the size of a bus, and it was smooth and black. Everything suggested that it had been parked there for a very long time, waiting.
When the news spread, many people around the world were frightened. Helen Ward spoke calmly on television and said that so far the relay had only sent messages, and that nobody had been harmed.
The relay explained that it was only a messenger. Its makers lived around Tau Lyra and called themselves the Choir, because they were made of light and sound.
Tau Lyra, the message said, was very old and growing colder every year. In about a hundred years its light would fade, and the Choir would fade with it.
The Choir did not ask to come to Earth, and they did not ask for help to escape. They asked for something much smaller and stranger: that someone would keep their Song.
The Song was everything the Choir had ever known. It held their history, their stories and the name of every one of them, stored inside the relay.
Kofi worked out that no single dish could catch so much sound at once. The only way was to link the radio dishes of many countries and listen together.
Anita Rao spent three days on the phone, calling every observatory she knew. Dozens agreed to help, and soon engineers arrived in Chile from every continent.

Not everyone was happy about the news, however, and in the capital some officials were worried. Helen Ward's bosses feared that the relay might be a trap, and they ordered the project closed until further notice.
Ines took a flight to Santiago to talk to Helen in person. She did not make a speech, but simply played her a small piece of the Song.
The fragment was a lullaby, and it reminded Helen of the songs her mother used to sing. When it ended, she wiped her eyes and said that she would find a way.
Helen Ward set three conditions that Ines gladly accepted. Everything would be open to the public, the dishes would only receive, and nobody would ever touch the relay.
For weeks, people worked day and night in the cold desert. Kofi led the cable crews, and he rarely slept, but he always had a joke ready.
As the Earth turned, the relay would be in view of dishes on every continent. However, the window was short, only six hours, and there would be no second chance.
The night before the window, a fierce storm swept over the Atacama and tore a cable from the biggest dish. At dawn Kofi climbed the tower in the wind and mended it with cold, shaking hands.
Everyone gathered in the control room as the countdown reached zero. Ines invited Luz to press the big green button, and across the world, the dishes turned together.
The Song began to arrive like a great river of sound, rich and layered and strange. Within an hour the copy had reached ten percent, and the room was silent.
By the third hour, the storage drives were almost full. Pavel put out a call for help, and thousands of people around the world lent the space on their own computers.
When the copy reached seventy percent, a new message from the Choir appeared. It warned that keeping the Song was not enough, and that it must also be played to stay alive.
The final part of the Song was a lullaby locked behind a puzzle. Pavel and Ines worked all night and discovered that the key was the simple tune that Luz had written.
Just before the six hours ended, the progress bar reached one hundred percent. The whole Song was safe on Earth, and for a long moment, nobody moved.
Far away, the dark relay's faint lights began to flicker. Then a last message arrived, and it was a goodbye.
The words said that the Choir was thankful, because it had been heard, and that nobody should be sad. Ines read them aloud to the quiet room and wiped her eyes.
That week the Song was played in public squares in cities all over the world. People stopped in the streets, and strangers held hands and listened.
Musicians around the world studied the Song and learned to play it on real instruments. In Prague, an orchestra performed it for the first time, and Pavel sat in the front row.
At last, the world decided to send an answer of its own to Tau Lyra. It was a gift of music and kind words, and it would take about twelve years to arrive.
Twenty-four years passed, and Luz grew into a scientist and a musician. One evening she returned to the same dish in the Atacama, where Kofi was still working.
The old screen flickered, and three soft notes arrived from Tau Lyra. They were the opening of the lullaby, and Luz knew at once what they meant: we hear you.
C1C2: High in the dry Atacama desert, where the stars burn without a flicker, Dr Ines Valdez sat alone beside a great white dish. For six years she had listened to the hiss of the sky on the night shift, and for six years it had told her nothing at all. She had learned to love the silence anyway, as one loves an old and unchanging friend.

Shortly after midnight, Kofi Adjei arrived with two cups of tea and a tired joke about the cold. Ines took one, glanced at her screen, and felt the warmth go out of her hands as she noticed a tiny, rhythmic ripple buried in the static. It seemed to be coming from a faint, distant star in the direction of Tau Lyra, far beyond the reach of any human traveller.

For a full hour the two of them stared at the screen without speaking, while the little pulse returned every seventy-three seconds with perfect precision. Natural sources of radio noise are restless and untidy, yet this one kept time like a metronome. Something, Ines thought, was tapping very gently on the glass of the sky, as if it hoped that somebody would be listening.

Because extraordinary claims deserve ordinary suspicion, Kofi swapped every cable, rebooted every computer and tested the receiver twice from top to bottom. Ines checked the weather, the power supply and even the radio of a passing truck. When they had run out of faults to blame, the pulse was still arriving, as calm as before.

At dawn Ines knocked on the door of the observatory's director, Anita Rao, and laid her records on the desk. Anita read them in silence, her eyebrows drawn together, for she had spent a long career watching exciting discoveries dissolve into dust. Her voice was gentle but firm when she said that wishes were not evidence.

In the end, Anita Rao decided that three days of quiet work could do no harm, and she made the team promise to tell nobody. She also sent a careful note to observatories on other continents, asking them to point their dishes at the same faint star. Her request did not say why, because she had no wish to start a panic over what might still be a mistake.

On the second morning a message arrived from a dish in the Australian outback, and Ines read it three times before she dared to believe it. Its operators had heard the identical pulse, every seventy-three seconds, from precisely the same point in the sky. Two machines on opposite sides of the world could not be wrong in the same way.

Ines sent the recordings to Dr Pavel Novak, a mathematician in Prague who adored puzzles and distrusted coincidence. By evening he was on the video link, nearly speechless, explaining that the pulses were counting out the prime numbers: two, three, five, seven, eleven. Nature, he said with a shaky laugh, has no reason to know what a prime number is, and certainly no reason to count them.

After the primes the signal paused, then began to paint a picture in tiny dots, one row at a time. When Pavel assembled it, they saw a star with a family of planets circling it, and a single world was marked as though to say, here we are. Nobody in the room breathed or spoke, and the only sound was the quiet hum of the machines around them.

That weekend, Ines's nine-year-old niece Luz came to stay at the observatory during her school holiday, bored and full of questions. To amuse her, Ines sped up the recording until the pulses became a stream of high, quick notes and let her listen through large headphones. The child fell silent at once, and her eyes slowly widened as the strange notes ran past her ears.

After a minute Luz opened her eyes and announced, with the certainty that only a nine-year-old possesses, that it was not a code at all but a song. She hummed the rising and falling notes back to her aunt, adding that the tune sounded sad and hopeful at the same time. Ines had spent a whole career looking at the sky as a puzzle of physics, and she had never once thought to listen to it as music.

Pavel spent the night comparing the notes against the dotted pictures, and by morning he had to admit that the child was right. Each musical phrase was paired with a small drawing, and each repetition added one tiny change, exactly as a patient teacher might introduce new words. Someone out there, across an enormous silence, was patiently trying to teach them how to talk.

Over the following days, the little team decoded the first words of the stranger's language, writing each new tune beside its picture on a wall of paper. Soon they could read we, you, near, far and listen, and each addition opened another door in a house that grew larger by the hour. Ines slept very little and smiled constantly, and she began to feel that she was learning to read the sky itself.

Secrets, like water, find the smallest crack, and within a week the news had leaked to the world. Reporters crowded the gate of the observatory, and a calm, direct woman named Dr Helen Ward arrived from the national science agency, carrying a thick folder of rules. She asked to see everything that the team had recorded, and she asked to be told the truth, whatever it turned out to be.

Helen made it clear that nobody could answer the signal without the approval of many people far above her, and she did not apologise for it. Ines understood the need for caution, yet she could not shake the fear that a long silence might be mistaken for a refusal. The two women regarded each other warily across the table, each of them wondering whether the other would turn out to be a friend.

One night, after weeks of patient work, Pavel decoded a complete sentence and read it aloud with a trembling voice. The senders had been listening to Earth's radio music for many years, it said, and now they humbly asked for an answer. The room was quiet for a long time after he had finished, as though the walls themselves were trying to take it in.

In a long and tense meeting, several officials argued that any reply might invite danger and that the safest course was to say nothing. Ines rose to her feet and pointed out, quietly, that silence is also a message, and that nobody wants to be ignored by a stranger who has come so far. Helen Ward watched her closely and said nothing at all, but her pencil had stopped moving across her notebook.

To everyone's surprise, Helen Ward decided that a short and gentle answer would be both honest and safe. Ines, Pavel and Luz composed it together over a long afternoon, and it contained the first few primes followed by a simple melody that Luz had written herself. It was the smallest and gentlest greeting that the whole of planet Earth could possibly send to a stranger.

At midnight the great dish swung slowly toward Tau Lyra, and the little greeting streamed out into the dark. Afterward the team sat together in the control room with their tea going cold, quietly calculating how many years they might have to wait. Nobody wanted to leave, and nobody could think of anything to say, so they simply listened to the faint hiss of the empty sky.

Less than four minutes after the greeting had gone out, the screen flickered and a fresh pattern began to arrive, bright and unmistakable. It was a reply, and it had come back in the time it takes to boil an egg. Ines stared at it with her heart pounding, because it simply could not be true.

Kofi chalked the figures on the whiteboard and checked them twice, then a third time, as though the arithmetic might change its mind. Light from Tau Lyra needs about twelve years to reach Earth, so whatever had answered so promptly could not be at the star at all. It had to be right on our cosmic doorstep, close enough that a person could almost imagine throwing a stone at it.

Astronomers in Hawaii aimed their largest telescope at the spot that Kofi's calculations had suggested, and after a long night they found something. A small, dark object was drifting about a million kilometres from Earth, roughly three times the distance of the Moon, and it reflected almost no light at all. It had been there, unseen and unsuspected, for a very long time, perhaps for longer than there had been telescopes on Earth.

When the images were sharpened, the object proved to be about the size of a bus, smooth and black and entirely without markings. Everything about it suggested a patient machine that had been parked in the dark for ages, listening to the radio chatter of a young and noisy planet. Because it seemed to be passing messages along from somewhere else, the team agreed to call it the relay.

When the news of the relay reached the public, fear spread across the planet like a cold wind, and some people began to talk of war. Helen Ward stood before the cameras and spoke with calm authority, reminding the world that the machine had so far done nothing but send kind words. Ines, watching from the back of the room, was surprised by how proud she felt of a woman she had once thought of as an obstacle.

Through a long and patient series of tunes, the relay explained that it was only a messenger, built to carry a voice across the dark. Its makers lived around the faint star Tau Lyra and called themselves the Choir, for they existed as shifting patterns of light and sound rather than as bodies. Pavel laughed aloud in delight, because a creature made of music was the most beautiful idea he had ever been told.

The relay went on to explain, in notes both tender and unafraid, that the Choir's star was very old and was slowly growing cold. Within about a hundred years its light would fail, and the Choir, who lived on that light, would gently fade away with it. Ines felt a lump rise in her throat as she tried to imagine a whole people growing quiet in the dark.

The Choir, it turned out, had no wish to cross the dark or to take anyone's home, and the relay said so clearly and more than once. Their request was far smaller and far stranger: they asked that someone, somewhere, would receive and keep their Song. They wished to be remembered, and that was all, and it was perhaps the most human wish that a stranger could have made.

The Song, Pavel gradually realised, was no ordinary piece of music but a whole civilisation folded into sound. It held their history and their stories, their scientific discoveries and their jokes, and the name of every single member of the Choir, and all of it lay waiting inside the relay. It was, quite simply, the largest and strangest library that anyone had ever offered to the people of Earth as a gift.

Kofi worked through the numbers and reached a sobering conclusion: no single dish on Earth could capture so enormous a Song during the short time the relay would be in view. The only solution was to link the radio dishes of many nations into one great ear. It had never been attempted at such a scale, and many experts privately doubted that it could be done at all.

Anita Rao, who had once demanded evidence, now spent three days on the telephone persuading every observatory she knew to join the effort. Dozens agreed, some within minutes, and engineers soon began to arrive in the Atacama from every continent with suitcases full of cables and tools. The desert, usually so empty and silent, suddenly hummed with the sound of voices speaking in a dozen different languages.

Not everyone shared the general enthusiasm, and in the capital a group of nervous officials decided that the relay might be a trap. They sent Helen Ward a firm letter ordering the project closed until further notice. She read it twice, folded it carefully, and sat for a long time without moving.

Ines flew to Santiago at once, determined not to argue but to share, and she met Helen in a small office with a speaker on the table. Instead of making a speech, she played a short fragment of the Song and let the music do the persuading. The room filled with a sound like moonlight made audible, a slow and silvery melody that seemed to rise from the very floor.

The fragment turned out to be a lullaby, and its gentle shape reminded Helen so strongly of the songs her mother had sung that her eyes filled with tears. When the last note faded, she was quiet for a moment, then said that she would find a way to protect the project. Sometimes, she reflected later, a melody can argue more persuasively than the finest speech that has ever been written.

Helen returned to her superiors with three firm conditions, which Ines accepted at once and without any hesitation. Everything would be done in the open, in front of the whole world, and the dishes would receive but never transmit anything beyond the original greeting, while the relay itself would remain untouched. With those promises written down and signed in front of witnesses, the project was allowed to continue after all.

For weeks, hundreds of engineers laboured day and night in the cold desert, laying cables, aligning dishes and testing software, while Kofi moved among them like a cheerful general. He hardly slept, and he gave up on shaving altogether, yet his jokes never ran out. Somehow, piece by piece and cable by cable, a worldwide ear was slowly taking shape beneath the desert stars.

Pavel's calculations showed that, as the Earth rotated, the relay would pass in view of dishes on every continent, but only for a window of about six hours. After that it would drift out of reach for months, and nobody could guarantee that the offer would still stand. The team understood perfectly well that they would have only one chance, and that nothing could be allowed to go wrong.

On the night before the great day, an unexpected storm swept across the Atacama and tore a critical cable from the largest dish. At first light Kofi strapped on his harness, climbed the swaying tower in the howling wind, and repaired it with numb and shaking hands. When he finally reached the ground again, grinning like a schoolboy, the whole crew stood and applauded his courage.

When the countdown reached zero, the control room was packed with engineers, officials and journalists, all of them holding their breath. Ines invited Luz to press the large green button, which the child did with immense seriousness, and all across the world, the great dishes turned as one. It looked like a vast field of white flowers turning their faces together to follow the sun across the sky.

The Song began to pour in like a river of silver, rich and layered and unlike anything that human instruments had ever produced. Within an hour the copy had reached ten percent, and the room, which a moment earlier had been full of nervous chatter, fell completely silent. Even the toughest and most practical engineers in the room found themselves blinking back tears at the sheer beauty of it.

By the third hour, the storage drives were almost full, and the stream showed no sign of slowing down. Pavel broadcast an urgent appeal for help, and within minutes, thousands of volunteers across the world offered the empty space on their own computers. Nobody had asked them in particular, and nobody could have stopped them, for generosity travels faster than any order.

When the copy reached seventy percent, a new message from the Choir appeared among the notes, urgent yet gentle in tone. It warned that merely storing the Song would be like keeping a seed in a drawer, and that for the Song to live, somebody must also learn to play it. The message ended with a few careful instructions, written in the same patient tunes that the Choir had used from the start.

The final section of the Song was a lullaby, but it was sealed behind a puzzle that nobody could solve, and the hours were running out. Pavel and Ines stared at it until their eyes ached, and then Luz hummed a few notes of her own tune, and the lock opened. The key had been hidden in plain sight all along, folded inside a child's simple melody that everybody had already heard.

Just minutes before the window closed, the progress bar crept to one hundred percent, and the Song was safe on Earth at last. For a long moment nobody moved or spoke or even seemed to breathe, and then the room erupted in cheers that were half laughter and half sobbing. Ines found that she was holding Luz's hand very tightly, and neither of them seemed to want to let go of the other.

Far above them, in the cold dark, the faint lights of the relay began to flicker softly, like a candle at the end of the evening. A last message came in, its notes slow and warm and clear, and Pavel translated it with a shaking voice. It was a goodbye, but it was spoken so tenderly that it felt more like a blessing than an ending.

The final words were simple and unforgettable: “Thank you, for we were heard, and so we shall not be sad.” Ines read them aloud to the silent room, and for once she did not mind that her voice shook. It seemed right that a farewell between two worlds should be both small and enormous.

That week, the first public recordings of the Song were played in town squares from Santiago to Seoul, and the cities themselves seemed to hold their breath. Commuters stopped on the pavement, shopkeepers came out of their doors, and strangers stood shoulder to shoulder in the evening light, listening to a civilisation sing. Many of them wept without quite knowing why, and others simply closed their eyes and swayed to the rhythm of the music.

In the weeks that followed, musicians around the world studied the Song and began to learn it on violins, flutes and human voices, for the Choir had asked for it to be played. In Prague an orchestra performed the first full movement, and Pavel sat in the front row with tears running freely down his face. The Choir, in a sense, was singing again, and this time the whole of humanity had come to sit and listen.

At last, with the world's blessing, Ines and her team prepared an answer to send back to Tau Lyra: a gift of Earth's music, stories and kind words. It would take about twelve years to reach the faint star, and another twelve for any reply to come home. Ines remarked with a smile that patience was a quality that astronomers learned very young, and that they never lost it afterward.

Twenty-four years passed, and the nine-year-old girl grew into a scientist and a musician with her aunt's stubbornness and her own quiet gift for listening. One evening she returned to the same great dish in the Atacama, where her old friend Kofi, now greying at the temples, was still making tea on the night shift. The desert sky glittered above them like a spilled jar of sugar, and the old dish turned slowly toward it as it always had.

Shortly after midnight the old screen flickered, and three soft notes arrived from the direction of Tau Lyra, as clear as a bell across a valley. They were the opening of the lullaby, and Luz, who had hummed it a thousand times, knew at once what they meant: we hear you. She smiled up at the glittering stars, took a deep breath, and began to sing back across the long, patient years.
